description: Team from Lima, Peru, turning open-source data into tools anyone can use. Space exploration starts on Earth.
summary: NovaTerra Labs is an open, data-driven search for Earth analogues of the two places exploration is actually heading to: the Shackleton crater rim near the lunar south pole (Artemis) and Jezero crater on Mars (Perseverance). Today, analogue sites are chosen mostly by tradition, not by data. We built a reproducible pipeline that measures four metrics (slope, roughness, aridity, and day–night temperature range) on the planetary targets (NASA LRO LOLA and Diviner, USGS Mars 2020 CTX DTM, Perseverance MEDA) and on Earth (Copernicus DEM, NASA POWER). It combines them into a 0–100 similarity index. We scored 15 sites and every 10 × 10 km cell of three search zones in Peru, Chile, and Argentina (1,265 cells). We checked the results with a 375-weight sensitivity test, unsupervised machine learning, and satellite imagery, and we state where the analogy breaks. Results: La Pampa de la Joya (Peru) ranks first for Mars (66.5), above the Atacama Desert. The Cerro Chao dacite dome (Chile) ranks first for the Moon (59.7). The algorithm also found a new, unnamed Atacama plain scoring 89.5. Everything can be explored in a browser app, so mission planners, rover teams, and students can find training grounds with evidence themselves.
details:
Project Details

What it does and how it works
Before a rover or a crew flies, it trains on Earth. Yet the usual analogue sites (Atacama, Haughton, Death Valley, Iceland, Hawaii) were chosen by tradition, and nobody has scored Earth’s surface against the places Artemis and Perseverance actually go. NovaTerra Labs does this automatically with open data and one method for three worlds:

  • Planetary targets: the Shackleton crater rim at the lunar south pole (NASA LRO LOLA 5 m topography, LRO Diviner temperatures) and Jezero crater on Mars (USGS Mars 2020 CTX DTM, Perseverance MEDA).
  • Earth: 15 sites (8 reference analogues and 7 new candidates), plus every 10 × 10 km land cell of three search zones in southern Peru, the Atacama–Altiplano (Chile) and the Puna de Catamarca (Argentina), 1,265 cells in total. Terrain comes from the Copernicus DEM GLO-30 and climate from NASA POWER (2015–2024).
  • Similarity index (0–100): slope, roughness, aridity and day–night temperature range (weights 0.3 / 0.3 / 0.3 / 0.1), computed the same way everywhere. The algorithm proposes and nobody picks squares by hand. Cells more than 50 km from our sites are flagged as new finds.

How we validate

  1. Sensitivity: across 375 weight sets, La Pampa de la Joya stays #1 for Mars in 78% of them and Cerro Chao #1 for the Moon in 89%.
  2. Machine learning: k-means (k = 3, chosen by silhouette score) groups the cells into terrain families without our weights. All 20 best Mars cells fall in the low-relief, hyper-arid family with La Joya and the Atacama.
  3. Imagery check: we review the top cells in Sentinel-2 and Google Earth and report what we see. For example, a small solar plant sits on the best Atacama cell.
  4. Where it breaks: no place on Earth has 0.17 g, a vacuum or 1.4 mSv/day. The index compares terrain and climate only, and each site lists its weakest match.

What we found

  • #1 Mars analogue (new candidate): La Pampa de la Joya, Arequipa, Peru, 66.5, above the Atacama Desert (56.7). Suited to rover driving, landing and navigation tests.
  • #1 Moon analogue (new candidate): Cerro Chao dacite dome, Chile, 59.7, above Lanzarote (37.7). Suited to EVA walking, slope mobility and lunar dome science.
  • New find: an unnamed Atacama plain, 89.5, 117 km from any known site, with a slope of 2.9° like Jezero’s. Confirmed on imagery.

The experience
A browser app with no installation and a guided tour takes the user through five steps: Bridge (choose Moon or Mars), Atlas (3D globe), Field Log (real 3D terrain next to the planetary target at the same scale), Compare (rankings, method, limits) and Discover (zone heat maps, ML families and live, approximate analysis of any place on Earth).

Benefits and impact
Mission planners, rover, lander and EVA teams get training grounds ranked with evidence instead of tradition. Students in Peru and Latin America discover analogues in their own backyard. Everything is open and reproducible: each score traces to a public dataset, the pipeline runs end to end in Google Colab, and adding a site or zone takes one line of code.

Tools
Figma · Python in Google Colab (rasterio, scikit-learn) · globe.gl, Leaflet, Plotly.js · HTML/CSS/JavaScript · GitHub and GitHub Pages · built with AI assistance: Claude (Anthropic).

Creativity and factors considered
We turned analogue selection into a search problem: one index applied the same way to the Moon, Mars and every square of Earth, so the algorithm can propose places nobody had scored. We focused on the real mission targets, tested the results with different weights and an independent ML method, and state openly the limits of any Earth analogue and where our data is approximate.
